summary: A proposal from MITRE and UCLA authors for helping new ARPANET users who were not tied to any server site. It supports the NIC's suggestion of a working group on user information and services and offers a specific idea for that group's meeting. The Resources Notebook was then the main source of network-wide information.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 462 responds to the need for better information about ARPANET services. It proposes that each server site maintain information about its own resources, with a way to access those files across the network.

questions: how to find services on the arpanet
subtitle: A proposal to let network sites maintain information about their own services.

tldr.problem: As the ARPANET gained users who were not attached to a server site, they needed information about network hosts and services. Compiling that information through many steps caused delay and errors.
tldr.mechanism: The authors support forming a working group on user information and propose a distributed database, with each server site maintaining a local information file and a later mechanism for accessing those files.
tldr.outcome: The RFC offers a proposal for discussion and leaves the access mechanism unspecified.

today: The unit records RFC 462's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. It is a proposal about collecting and accessing network-service information.

sections.title: Helping New Network Users
sections.content:
The ARPANET was moving toward serving a larger group of users, including terminal users who were not associated with a server site. They needed information about which network hosts offered services and how people could access them.

The Resources Notebook was then the main source of network-wide information. The authors support the NIC's suggestion to form a Working Group concerned with User Information and Services and offer a proposal for it to consider.
sections.plainLanguage: New users needed a clear way to learn which network computers offered services. The authors support creating a group to address that need.

sections.title: Put Information Near Its Source
sections.content:
The authors say that collecting basic information through many steps uses too many people, delays the result and introduces errors. They propose placing information gathering and maintenance closer to its source, so each server site takes responsibility for its own information.

The proposed network database would be distributed and extensible. Each site would maintain an information file locally and/or at the NIC. The RFC presents a mechanism for accessing these files as a later step, not a defined part of this proposal.
sections.plainLanguage: Each site knows its own services, so the authors propose that each site keep its information current. A later step would define how people and tools find those separate files.

sections.title: Making Different Files Accessible
sections.content:
The authors expect people at different sites to use whichever tools are comfortable and available to them. One technical question is how an automated tool could access information stored in different files.

The RFC notes that the NIC was trying to smooth the interface between NLS and non-NLS files. The authors identify that work as a reasonable target for efforts to make the proposed information easier to access.
sections.plainLanguage: Sites might store information in different kinds of files. The proposal points to a shared access method as a problem to solve, but does not specify one.
